title: Iowa City Mother of Four Deported to Sierra Leone Before a Judge Heard Her Case
excerpt: Fatou Traore, in the US for over 20 years and protected from return to Ivory Coast since 2011, was removed to a country she has never visited, advocates say.
body:
• Fatou Traore, an Iowa City mother of four who has lived in the United States for more than 20 years, was deported to Sierra Leone on October 13, according to advocacy group Escucha Mi Voz.
  • Advocates say she was removed without appearing before an immigration judge, despite a 2011 order barring her deportation to her home country, Ivory Coast.
  • She was arrested by ICE on September 24 on her way to work and held in Louisiana; her children, aged 3 to 19, remain in Iowa.
  • Lawyers in Sierra Leone, New York and Iowa City are working to bring her back so her case can be heard; her attorney says she may be sent onward to Ivory Coast within two weeks.

An Iowa City mother of four was deported on Tuesday to Sierra Leone, a country advocates say she has never visited and has no ties to, without first appearing before an immigration judge. Fatou Traore had lived in the United States for more than two decades, according to the Iowa City Press-Citizen, which reported the announcement by immigration advocacy group Escucha Mi Voz.

Arrested on the way to work

Escucha Mi Voz said Traore was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement on September 24 while on her way to work in Iowa City. She was held at Richwood Correctional Center in Monroe, Louisiana, before her removal. Her four children, the youngest aged three, are in Iowa. Her son Esoumaila Diallo said in the group's statement that she had asked for a chance to have her case heard and for a fear interview before any removal.

https://x.com/gazettedotcom/status/2110037345391239521

"My mother asked for a chance to have her case heard. They deported her before a judge ruled."

— Esoumaila Diallo, Traore's son, via Escucha Mi Voz

A 2011 protection, and a disputed record

In 2011 Traore was granted withholding of removal to Ivory Coast, a protection given when an immigration judge finds a person would likely face persecution if returned there. Court filings reported by the Press-Citizen show she challenged her removal on the basis of that stay and on fear of torture and persecution. ICE told another Iowa outlet that she had admitted using a fake birth certificate and passport to enter the United States. Her family has denied those allegations, and faith leaders supporting her say she has no criminal history. The Executive Office for Immigration Review did not immediately respond to a request for comment, the Press-Citizen reported.

Her removal to a third country rather than to Ivory Coast follows a recent Supreme Court ruling that allows the administration to deport people to countries other than their own, according to Iowa reporting on the case.

Bipartisan appeals that did not stop the removal

The case drew an unusual breadth of local support. Republican Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks wrote to the Department of Homeland Security asking for a stay, and her Democratic challenger Christina Bohannan also called for Traore's release, the Press-Citizen reported in earlier coverage of the appeals. Senator Chuck Grassley said he would have an immigration expert in his office review the case. Three Iowa bishops — Lutheran, Methodist and Catholic — also appealed to Homeland Security, and more than 100 community members marched to a federal building in Cedar Rapids on October 7. Davenport Bishop Dennis Walsh called the planned removal, in a letter reported by Catholic World Report, a grave injustice.

What happens next

Attorney Alma David told the Press-Citizen she took on the case after the deportation, has spoken with Traore by phone, and believes Traore is likely to be sent from Sierra Leone to Ivory Coast within the next two weeks. A legal team is working to return her to the United States so she can receive due process. For immigrant families watching the case, the practical lesson is stark: a long-standing withholding order and pending fear claims did not, in this instance, pause a removal, so anyone with a similar order should confirm its status with counsel before any ICE check-in or travel.
